title: Workshop Overview
content:
What You Will Build ReLoop connects device owners with verified repair and recycling partners while screening uploaded device photos with multimodal AI so listings stay clean, structured, and accurate. In this workshop you deploy the complete reloop2 stack using strictly serverless AWS services—zero EC2 instances, zero NAT Gateways, and pay-per-request scaling down to near zero when idle.
End-to-End Request Flows Static Web Delivery (/, all SPA routes): Browser connects over HTTPS -> Edge WAF (reloop2-web in us-east-1) -> CloudFront Distribution (PriceClass_200) -> CloudFront Function reloop2-spa-rewrite rewrites extensionless routes to /index.html while keeping dotted chat URLs (<partnerId>.<listingId>) intact -> private S3 web bucket via Origin Access Control (OAC). API & Authentication Calls (/api/*): Browser calls CloudFront /api/* -> CloudFront Function reloop2-api-prefix strips the /api prefix -> CloudFront forwards to HTTP API Gateway (reloop2-api in ap-southeast-1) injecting a shared secret header x-origin-verify -> API Gateway verifies JWT against Cognito (ANY /{proxy+}) or passes public routes -> Lambda (reloop2-api, Node.js 22 ARM64) validates x-origin-verify with timingSafeEqual and reads/writes DynamoDB. Direct Browser Image Upload & AI Analysis: Authenticated user requests a presigned upload from Lambda -> Browser uploads photo straight to private S3 bucket (reloop2-images-<suffix>) tagged state=pending -> On listing inspection, Lambda invokes Amazon Rekognition (DetectModerationLabels + DetectText OCR) -> screens extracted text with Amazon Bedrock Guardrail (ApplyGuardrailCommand) -> invokes Amazon Bedrock (global.moonshotai.kimi-k3) ConverseCommand to return structured device fields (title, category, brand, model, condition, defect description). Scheduled Maintenance & Alerts: Every 15 minutes, Amazon EventBridge rule reloop2-sweep invokes reloop2-api to expire 7-day open listings, issue 24-hour pickup reminders, and auto-complete 48-hour handoffs. CloudWatch Logs (7-day retention), a custom metric filter (UnhandledErrors), two CloudWatch metric alarms, SNS email alerts, and ReLoop2-Backend-Health provide live operational visibility. Security Highlights Layer Protection Mechanism Edge Network reloop2-web WAFv2 (CloudFront, us-east-1): 100 req/min rate limit on public endpoints, 1,000 req/min global IP ceiling, AWS IP Reputation List, Known Bad Inputs, Common Rule Set Browser Headers CloudFront Response Headers Policy (reloop2-security-headers): HSTS (max-age=31536000), X-Frame-Options: DENY, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin, enforced frame-ancestors 'none' + CSP-Report-Only Origin Protection Both S3 buckets have Block Public Access ON (s3-web OAC-only, s3-images presigned-only); Lambda rejects any API request missing matching x-origin-verify header Identity Cognito User Pool protected by regional WAF reloop2-auth (ap-southeast-1, 300 auth calls / 5 min / IP), Pre-SignUp duplicate email guard, Deletion Protection ACTIVE, Auth Code PKCE Least Privilege IAM Separate Lambda execution roles (reloop2-post-confirmation-role and reloop2-api-lambda-role) scoped to explicit table ARNs, listings/* prefix, and required AI actions Workshop Cost Estimate Running the entire workshop from build through live E2E verification takes roughly 2–3 hours and is followed by a clean teardown in Module 5.13:
Service Usage During Workshop Estimated Cost DynamoDB On-demand reads/writes (<5 MB stored, PITR) ~$0.01 (Free Tier covers most) S3 Two private buckets, <20 MB assets & test photos <$0.01 Lambda & HTTP API Gateway ~100–300 invocations, 512 MB ARM64 $0.00 (Free Tier) Cognito Essentials tier, 1–5 test users $0.00 (Free Tier: 10,000 MAU) CloudFront <1 GB transfer, 2 CloudFront Functions $0.00 (Free Tier: 1 TB/mo) AWS WAFv2 2 Web ACLs x 7 rules prorated for ~1 day + 1K requests ~$0.25–$0.50 (or ~$12/mo if left running 30 days!) Bedrock & Rekognition ~5–15 test image moderations + Kimi K3 calls ~$0.05–$0.30 Total for Workshop Built, verified E2E, and deleted same day < $1.00 USD AWS WAFv2 Web ACLs charge $5/month per ACL + $1/month per rule continuously even with zero traffic. Complete Module 5.13 right after finishing Module 5.12 so your monthly bill remains minimal.

title: Blog 1
content:
One Chair, Two People, and an Unforgiving Database Imagine a platform connecting customers with service partners, where each job can only be accepted by one person. Partner A and Partner B see the same listing, and both click “Accept Job” almost simultaneously.
If the backend handles it naively:
Check if the job is still available. If available, update the assignee. Congratulations, you’ve just assigned two owners to a single job. One chair, two people trying to sit at once.
How to Solve This?
Instead of having two sides negotiate with each other, we appoint Amazon DynamoDB as the strict gatekeeper:
AWS Lambda receives the request and builds a transaction using TransactWriteItems. DynamoDB executes two atomic operations in the same transaction: it updates the job status only if its current state is OPEN, and simultaneously persists an Idempotency Key to guard against duplicate processing. Only one transaction wins the job. The competing transaction receives a conditional check failure/conflict error. If the winner resends the request due to a network timeout, the backend reads the stored idempotency result rather than re-executing side effects. The elegance here is that we don’t need to guess who clicked a few milliseconds faster. The database decides deterministically based on real-time state at the exact moment of write.
What Needs Verification?
Fire two concurrent requests from different users targeting the same job record. The expected outcome is that exactly one user claims the job. Then, replay the winner’s request and verify that no duplicate side effects are triggered.
One transaction, one winner, no human referee required.
Note: This architecture and testing design is a proposed pattern.

title: Blog 2
content:
You Have a Valid Passport, But Do You Have the Right to Renovate Your Neighbor’s House? There is an intriguing security vulnerability in web application development that is easy to overlook. A user signs in successfully, provides a cryptographically valid token, and the API responds normally. But does that mean they have the right to edit every post in the system? Absolutely not.
Consider this scenario:
User A logs in successfully. User B creates a post with ID 123. User A issues a PATCH /posts/123 request to update B’s post. If the backend only verifies that the JWT signature is valid, User A can alter User B’s data at will (IDOR vulnerability).
Two Distinct Concepts
Authentication: Who are you? Authorization: What are you permitted to do with this specific resource? How to Solve This?
An architectural pattern that handles this cleanly:
Amazon Cognito manages user identities and issues signed JWTs. API Gateway JWT Authorizer verifies token authenticity before the request ever reaches backend compute. AWS Lambda extracts the caller’s unique sub from the verified token claims, rather than trusting any ownerId sent in the request payload. When updating the record, Lambda issues a DynamoDB UpdateItem guarded by a condition expression: ownerId = :callerSub. If the caller is not the owner, the condition fails atomically and the operation is rejected.
Key takeaway: Hiding the Edit button on the frontend is NOT security. An attacker can always forge HTTP calls directly against the endpoint.
What Needs Verification?
Log in with User A’s credentials, use A’s valid token to attempt modifying User B’s post. The expected result is successful authentication but strict authorization failure (403 Forbidden).
Holding a valid passport doesn’t mean you own every house in the city.
Note: This architecture and testing design is a proposed pattern.

title: Proposal
content:
RELOOP An AI-assisted marketplace for used and broken electronics, built serverless on AWS 1. Executive Summary ReLoop is a web marketplace where people in Vietnam sell used or broken electronics (phones, laptops, monitors, components) to nearby repair shops, buyers and recyclers. It was built by AWSS3nt1n4L, a 5-person team in the AWS First Cloud Journey (FCAJ) program in Ho Chi Minh City, during a 12-week internship (14/09–04/12/2026). A seller uploads photos, and Amazon Bedrock pre-fills the listing. The listing then goes to every approved buyer whose branch service area (1–15 km) covers it, and the deal closes through a buyer quote or a price agreed in chat. On 08/11/2026 the dev environment had 14 registered accounts, 12 active listings from 7 sellers and about 31,000 API requests over the first month. The serverless design scales without re-architecture: Lambda concurrency is approved up to 1,000. The core services are CloudFront, AWS WAF, API Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB, S3, Cognito, Rekognition, Bedrock, EventBridge, CloudWatch and SNS. Guests can browse the market without an account. Signed-in users can chat and buy. Only Admin-approved partners can sell, and only Admin and Finance Admin can moderate content and handle invoices.
Team Member Role Kung Cẩm Thành Team Lead Hoàng Quốc Việt Tech Lead Trần Hoàng Quốc Trung Backend Engineer Nguyễn Duy Quang Frontend Engineer Nguyễn Anh Kỳ Cyber-security / Documentation 2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? The Global E-waste Monitor 2024 (UNITAR/ITU) reports that the world generated 62 million tonnes of e-waste in 2022, and only 22.3% was formally collected and recycled. The same report estimates that Vietnam generated about 516,000 tonnes (≈5.3 kg per person) in 2022. Owners of an old or broken device rarely know who will take it or what it is worth. Today they post on general classifieds sites or social groups, describe the device by hand, call shops one by one, and often get no answer. General marketplaces such as Chợ Tốt or Facebook Marketplace are built for any kind of goods. They do not:
match a listing to the shops whose service area covers the seller, show a price estimate from the buyer’s own pricing rules, keep a reputation record that rewards buyers who honour their quotes. Small repair shops face the same gap from the other side. They have no cheap channel to receive nearby devices that fit what they buy.
The Solution ReLoop runs the whole flow on managed AWS services. There are no servers to run.
Ingest: the browser uploads up to 6 photos per listing (JPEG/PNG/WebP, max 5 MB each) straight to Amazon S3 using presigned POST URLs. Amazon Rekognition checks every photo for unsafe content and reads any text in it. That text goes through Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, so prompt-injection attempts are flagged for Admin review.
Processing: one AWS Lambda function (Node.js 22, arm64) serves 111 API routes behind Amazon API Gateway. It also calls itself asynchronously for slow work:
AI photo analysis with Kimi K3 on Bedrock, about 35 s per run; geohash + Haversine matching of listings to buyer branches. Amazon EventBridge triggers the same function every 15 minutes to expire listings, auto-complete transactions after 48 hours, send reminders and issue monthly invoices.
Storage: a single Amazon DynamoDB table (PK/SK + one GSI) stores every entity: users, partners, branches, pricing rules, listings, quotes, transactions, chats, reviews, invoices and audit logs. Writes are conditional, and money-related APIs require an Idempotency-Key. S3 lifecycle rules delete unused photos after 1 day and all photos after 90 days.
Interface: a React single-page app served from a private S3 bucket through Amazon CloudFront. It has a public market, a partner portal (2 tiers) and an Admin portal.
Security: Amazon Cognito handles sign-in with Admins / FinanceAdmins groups. API Gateway checks a JWT on every private route. Two AWS WAF web ACLs protect the site: one on CloudFront (managed rules + rate limits) and one on the Cognito user pool (login rate limit). A strict Content-Security-Policy is applied, and each IAM permission is limited to exactly what the code needs.
Compared with general classifieds, ReLoop adds AI-filled listings, service-area matching, rule-based price estimates, a two-step completion (seller confirms the final price, buyer accepts) and two-way reviews. ReLoop does not handle payment: buyer and seller pay each other in person at hand-over.
Benefits and Return on Investment Less manual input: AI suggests title, category, brand, model and condition from up to 3 photos. The seller only confirms or edits. A listing takes about 5 minutes by hand versus under 1 minute with AI (team estimate). Fewer unanswered listings: every new listing is matched automatically to all buyer branches in range, and listings within 5 km are ranked first. Reliability: state machines, conditional writes and idempotent background jobs keep listings, quotes and transactions consistent. 182 automated tests and an end-to-end smoke test run against AWS. Learning value: the team practised single-table DynamoDB design, event-driven Lambda, Bedrock structured output, Terraform IaC, WAF tuning and an automated pentest. Cost: about 18.70 USD/month (224.40 USD/year) at the current scale (section 6). 17.00 USD of that is AWS WAF, so without WAF the platform costs about 1.70 USD/month. Until 28/02/2027 the cost is covered by the account’s remaining credits (197.14 USD on 08/11/2026). Payback: revenue is 10,000 VND per completed transaction, paid by the seller. At an assumed rate of 1 USD ≈ 26,000 VND (approximate rate, November 2026), 18.70 USD ≈ 486,200 VND. The platform therefore breaks even at 49 completed transactions per month, or 5 per month without WAF. 3. Solution Architecture ReLoop is fully serverless in one region (ap-southeast-1):
All browser traffic passes AWS WAF and CloudFront. Static files come from a private S3 bucket, and /api/* is forwarded to an HTTP API with a secret origin header, so direct calls to API Gateway are rejected. One Lambda function holds the business logic. It calls DynamoDB, S3, Rekognition and Bedrock through small adapters, so the same code also runs locally on Node.js with in-memory storage. Sign-up and sign-in go directly from the browser to Cognito, protected by a second WAF. Logs and custom business metrics flow to CloudWatch, and alarms are sent to the Admin by SNS email. All infrastructure is defined in Terraform, with state stored in a versioned S3 bucket. Diagram source: static/images/2-Proposal/reloop-architecture.drawio (generated by diagram/make_architecture.py).
AWS Services Used Amazon CloudFront: serves the web app and routes /api/* to API Gateway. It adds CSP, HSTS and X-Frame-Options headers and returns a real 404 for missing static files. AWS WAF: 2 web ACLs. reloop-dev-web on CloudFront: 3 AWS managed rule groups plus 2 rate limits returning 429. The limits are 100 requests per minute per IP on the public API and 1,000 requests per minute per IP overall. reloop-dev-auth on Cognito: 300 sign-in attempts per 5 minutes per IP, plus IP reputation. Amazon S3: 3 buckets — web bundle (private, OAC), device photos (presigned POST/GET, tag-based lifecycle) and Terraform state (versioned). Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API): JWT authorizer on every private route; throttled at 20 requests/s with a burst of 50. AWS Lambda: reloop-dev-api, Node.js 22 on arm64 (Graviton) with 512 MB. It runs the API, the async AI/matching worker, the scheduled jobs and the Cognito pre sign-up trigger. Average duration is 144 ms; concurrency quota is 1,000. Amazon DynamoDB: one on-demand table with PK/SK and GSI1, PITR and TTL (notifications expire after 90 days). It holds about 5,600 items (2.4 MB). Amazon Cognito: user pool with email verification and groups Admins, FinanceAdmins, Partners and Owners. It has 14 users. Amazon Rekognition: moderation labels on every photo (rejects explicit content; borderline cases go to Admin) and text detection. Amazon Bedrock: Kimi K3 through the Converse API with tool choice, returning structured JSON. A Guardrail (Standard tier) screens AI input/output and text found in photos. Each user is capped at 20 analyses per day. Amazon EventBridge: 1 rule every 15 minutes that runs the background sweep. Amazon CloudWatch: logs kept 7 days, custom business metrics, 1 dashboard and 10 alarms (Lambda errors/throttles, API 5xx, p95 > 2 s, AI/job failures, unusual photo text, new disputes). Amazon SNS: sends alarm emails to Admin. AWS IAM: one execution role scoped to the core table, the photo prefix, the specific Bedrock model and Guardrail, Rekognition, self-invoke and logs. AWS Security Agent: automated black-box pentest of the dev site (3.63 task-hours on 08/11/2026). Component Design Edge / Client: a React 18 + TypeScript SPA (Vite) with Leaflet + OpenStreetMap for picking locations. Guests see the market. After sign-in, users see the partner portal (tier 1: individual sellers, max 3 open listings; tier 2: businesses with branches, pricing rules and quotes, max 10) or the Admin portal. Ingestion: POST /uploads/presign returns a 5-minute presigned POST, and the browser uploads the photo directly to S3. POST /uploads/moderate runs Rekognition and tags the photo moderation=passed. When a listing is created, its photos are tagged state=attached, so the lifecycle rule keeps them. Processing: an HTTP router handles JWT claims, idempotency keys and input checks. Domain state machines for Listing, Quote and Transaction allow only valid moves (for example, a transaction cancel takes effect after 5 minutes, and completion is auto-accepted after 48 hours). AI analysis and matching run as async self-invocations. A job runner keyed by “time buckets” finds due work without table scans. Storage: all access patterns are listed in backend/src/store/keys.ts; the code never scans the table. The market feed is partitioned by month and paginated with a validated cursor. Money is stored as integer VND. Web Interface: the public market, chat per listing (5-second polling) with price offers, the transaction drawer (schedule hand-over, adjust price, confirm, dispute) and reviews. User Management: Cognito sign-up with email verification. The pre sign-up trigger blocks one mailbox from opening several accounts through email aliases (name+1@…, dotted Gmail addresses). Admin approves partner applications, and Finance Admin issues and settles monthly invoices. If an invoice is more than 3 days overdue the seller cannot post new listings; after 7 days the account is locked. Monitoring: structured JSON logs, metric filters for business events, a dashboard (reloop-dev-overview), alarms to SNS email, and WAF logs to CloudWatch Logs with authorization and cookie fields redacted. 4. title: DynamoDB Single-Table Data Layer
content:
ReLoop uses an Amazon DynamoDB single-table schema (reloop2-core-table) in ap-southeast-1 with On-Demand capacity, one Global Secondary Index (GSI1) for role/status queries, 35-day Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR), and Time to Live (TTL) for automatic cleanup of temporary records and timers.
Single-Table Key Design Overview Attribute Type Role PK String (S) Partition Key — entity prefix (USER#<id>, LISTING#<id>, TIMER#<isoTime>, SESSION#<id>) SK String (S) Sort Key — record subtype (PROFILE, META, QUOTE#<id>, LISTING_EXPIRE#<id>) GSI1PK String (S) Secondary partition key (ROLE#Owner, STATUS#OPEN, PARTNER#<id>) GSI1SK String (S) Secondary sort key (USER#<id>, <createdAt>) ttl Number (N) Unix epoch timestamp (seconds) monitored by DynamoDB TTL Step 1 — Create reloop2-core-table Switch back to Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1, open DynamoDB -> Tables, and click Create table. Under Table details: Table name: reloop2-core-table Partition key: PK (String) Sort key: SK (String) Select Customize settings, set Capacity mode to On-demand, then scroll to Secondary indexes -> click Create global index: Partition key: GSI1PK (String) Sort key: GSI1SK (String) Index name: GSI1 Attribute projections: All Review the complete configuration summary (On-demand throughput + Standard table class + GSI1). Confirm Secondary indexes shows GSI1 queued with ALL projection. Under Tags, add standard workshop tags: Owner = team Project = reloop2 Purpose = workshop Then click Create table. Wait ~15 seconds while the table status transitions from Creating to Active. Step 2 — Enable Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) & TTL Open reloop2-core-table -> Backups tab -> under Point-in-time recovery (PITR) click Edit. Check Turn on point-in-time recovery and set Recovery window (days) to 35, then click Save changes. Scroll to Additional settings -> Time to Live (TTL) -> click Turn on -> enter TTL attribute name: ttl -> Turn on TTL. Step 3 — Verify Table & Index Status Open the Overview tab and Indexes tab of reloop2-core-table to confirm: Status is Active Billing mode is On-demand GSI1 is Active with PK/SK + GSI1PK/GSI1SK (ALL)

title: Blog 3
content:
The Partner Has Closed the App, But Work Still Has to Find Them A familiar challenge: A customer posts a service request, and the system needs to match qualified partners and send quote invitations. But the partner is currently offline. Their app is closed, their phone is resting on the table.
Must we wait until they come online to dispatch the invitation? Not at all. We build a decoupled, event-driven system where the backend executes reliably regardless of user connectivity.
Proposed Architecture
Customer submits a request via Amazon API Gateway. AWS Lambda persists the job record in DynamoDB and emits a JobCreated event to Amazon EventBridge. EventBridge routes the event into Amazon SQS for durable asynchronous buffering. A Lambda Matcher worker queries eligible partners via DynamoDB Global Secondary Indexes (GSIs) filtered by geohash and service category. The worker writes individual offer invitations into an Offers table, using compound key partnerId + jobId to prevent duplicates. Amazon SNS sends push notifications as optional alerts—never as the primary data store. The Key Insight
State is saved first; notifications are delivered second. Even if the partner was offline during job creation, the invitation rests safely in the database. When they reopen the app, frontend queries GET /my-offers, and backend returns all persisted offers.
We don’t gamble on push notifications arriving reliably. A push notification is merely a knock on the door; DynamoDB holds the letter.
What if EventBridge replays events, or SQS delivers a message twice? Idempotent conditional writes prevent duplicate offers. Poison messages failing retries route safely to a Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) for inspection.
What Needs Verification?
Create a job while the candidate partner is offline. Verify that the offer record is persisted in DynamoDB. Open the app subsequently and confirm the offer renders correctly. Replay the exact event payload multiple times to prove offers are never duplicated. Inject an unparseable payload to verify DLQ redirection. A resilient system finishes its work without depending on 24/7 client connectivity.
Note: This architecture and testing design is a proposed pattern.

title: Cognito Authentication & Profile Sync
content:
In this module you configure Amazon Cognito (reloop2-user-pool), define RBAC user groups (Admins, FinanceAdmins, Partners, Owners), enable Managed Login v2 on domain reloop2-auth, and create the Python 3.12 Post-Confirmation Lambda (reloop2-post-confirmation) that writes every newly verified user straight into reloop2-core-table.
Part A — Create User Pool & Configure Authentication Open Amazon Cognito -> User pools in ap-southeast-1 and click Create user pool. In the Set up your application wizard: Choose Single-page application (SPA) Name your application client reloop2-web-client Select Email as the sign-in identifier and email, name as required sign-up attributes, then click Create user directory. Once Cognito creates the pool, review the generated User Pool ID and click Go to overview. On Overview, click Rename, enter reloop2-user-pool, and save. Under Authentication -> Authentication methods: verify Password (PASSWORD) is enabled and MFA is No MFA (Essentials tier default for smoother workshop onboarding; enable TOTP/SMS for production). Under Authentication -> Sign-in: confirm Email sign-in (alias_attributes = ["email"]) and case-insensitive usernames. Under Sign-up -> Attribute verification and user account confirmation: ensure self-service sign-up is on, email verification is active, and Account recovery uses Email only (verified_email, priority 1). Add workshop tags (Owner = team, Project = reloop2, Purpose = workshop) and confirm Deletion protection is Active (we will deactivate it explicitly in Module 5.13). Part B — Create User Groups (RBAC) Go to User management -> Groups and create all 4 groups: Group Name Precedence Description Admins 1 System operators and verifiers FinanceAdmins 1 Finance reconcilers (bank / payout approvals) Partners 2 Verified recycling and repair shops Owners 3 Device sellers Part C — Configure App Client (reloop2-web-client) & Managed Login Domain Open Applications -> App clients -> reloop2-web-client: check Authentication flows allow ALLOW_USER_SRP_AUTH and ALLOW_REFRESH_TOKEN_AUTH, access/ID token validity is 60 minutes, refresh token validity is 5 days, and Prevent user existence errors is enabled. Click the Login pages tab -> Edit Managed Login pages configuration: Temporarily set Allowed callback URLs to http://localhost:5173/auth/callback Temporarily set Allowed sign-out URLs to http://localhost:5173/ (we will append the CloudFront HTTPS URL in Module 5.8 once CloudFront is created!) OAuth 2.0 grant types: Authorization code grant (code) OpenID Connect scopes: openid, email, phone Go to Branding -> Domain. Cognito creates an auto-generated domain initially; create/replace with custom Cognito prefix reloop2-auth using Managed login version 2 (https://reloop2-auth.auth.ap-southeast-1.amazoncognito.com). Part D — Create Post-Confirmation IAM Role & Python Lambda When a user confirms their sign-up email code, Cognito synchronously calls reloop2-post-confirmation to insert their default Owner profile row into reloop2-core-table.
Open IAM -> Roles -> Create role: Trusted entity type: AWS service -> Lambda Attach AWS managed policy AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole (if your lab account requires a Permissions Boundary policy such as TeamAppRoleBoundary, select it under Permissions boundary; personal accounts leave none). Set Role name: reloop2-post-confirmation-role, add tags, and click Create role. Open reloop2-post-confirmation-role -> Add permissions -> Create inline policy (JSON): { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "PutUserProfile", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "dynamodb:PutItem", "Resource": "arn:aws:dynamodb:ap-southeast-1:123456789012:table/reloop2-core-table" } ] } Name the inline policy DynamoDBWriteAccess and save. Now open AWS Lambda -> Create function: Author from scratch Function name: reloop2-post-confirmation Runtime: Python 3.12 Architecture: x86_64 Execution role: Use an existing role -> reloop2-post-confirmation-role Upload or deploy the Python handler lambda_function.py (reloop2-post-confirmation.zip), then click Save: import datetime import os import boto3 dynamodb = boto3.client("dynamodb") TABLE_NAME = os.environ["TABLE_NAME"] def lambda_handler(event, context): if event.get("triggerSource") != "PostConfirmation_ConfirmSignUp": return event attrs = event["request"]["userAttributes"] user_id = attrs["sub"] email = attrs.get("email", "") name = attrs.get("name", "Unknown") role = "Owner" timestamp = datetime.datetime.utcnow().isoformat() + "Z" try: dynamodb.put_item( TableName=TABLE_NAME, Item={ "PK": {"S": f"USER#{user_id}"}, "SK": {"S": "PROFILE"}, "GSI1PK": {"S": f"ROLE#{role}"}, "GSI1SK": {"S": f"USER#{user_id}"}, "email": {"S": email}, "fullName": {"S": name}, "role": {"S": role}, "status": {"S": "ACTIVE"}, "createdAt": {"S": timestamp}, }, ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(PK)", ) except Exception as exc: print(f"Failed to write user to DynamoDB: {exc}") return event Verify Configuration -> General configuration (128 MB, 3 sec timeout) and add Environment variable: Key: TABLE_NAME Value: reloop2-core-table Part E — Attach Post-Confirmation Trigger in Cognito Return to Cognito User Pool reloop2-user-pool -> Extensions -> Lambda triggers, and click Add Lambda trigger. Configure: Trigger type: Sign-up Sign-up trigger: Post confirmation trigger Lambda function: reloop2-post-confirmation Then click Add Lambda trigger (Cognito automatically adds the Lambda resource-based invoke permission).

title: S3 Private Images, CORS & Lifecycle
content:
Uploaded device photos go directly from the user’s browser to a private Amazon S3 bucket (reloop2-images-<suffix>, e.g. reloop2-images-7k3q) via short-lived presigned URLs issued by Lambda. Block All Public Access stays enabled so photos cannot be listed or hotlinked outside controlled presigned URLs, while CORS allows browser uploads and S3 Lifecycle rules automatically purge abandoned pending uploads and incomplete multipart uploads.
Step 1 — Create Private Bucket reloop2-images-<suffix> Open Amazon S3 -> Buckets in ap-southeast-1 and click Create bucket. Configure General configuration: AWS Region: ap-southeast-1 Bucket type: General purpose Bucket name: reloop2-images-7k3q (replace 7k3q with your own globally unique 4-character suffix) Leave Block all public access checked (ON) — never expose raw user photos via public bucket policies. Add workshop tags (Owner=team, Project=reloop2, Purpose=workshop), keep SSE-S3 (AES256) with Bucket Key Enabled, and click Create bucket. Step 2 — Configure CORS for Direct Browser Uploads Open reloop2-images-7k3q -> Permissions -> scroll to Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) -> click Edit and paste (we start with http://localhost:5173, then append our CloudFront origin in Module 5.8): [ { "AllowedHeaders": ["*"], "AllowedMethods": ["PUT", "POST", "GET"], "AllowedOrigins": ["http://localhost:5173"], "ExposeHeaders": ["ETag"] } ] Step 3 — Add 3 Cost-Control Lifecycle Rules Open Management -> Lifecycle rules -> click Create lifecycle rule for each rule below: Rule Name Scope / Filter Action reloop2-listing-images-unattached Prefix listings/ AND object tag state = pending Expire current versions after 1 day reloop2-listing-images-retention Prefix listings/ (all attached photos) Expire current versions after 90 days reloop2-abort-incomplete-uploads Prefix listings/ Abort incomplete multipart uploads after 1 day Confirm all 3 lifecycle rules show status Enabled under Management -> Lifecycle rules.

title: AI Content Safety with Bedrock Guardrails
content:
ReLoop runs a multi-stage screening pipeline whenever a user analyzes device photos:
Amazon Rekognition (DetectModerationLabels + DetectText) runs on the S3 photo in ap-southeast-1. Any text detected by OCR (for example printed labels, serial stickers, or offensive text injected into a photo) is screened through Amazon Bedrock Guardrail (reloop2-ai-guardrail) via ApplyGuardrailCommand. If screening passes, Amazon Bedrock (global.moonshotai.kimi-k3) executes ConverseCommand to inspect the device photos and return structured JSON attributes. Important Runtime Note on Kimi K3: In Bedrock Runtime (index.js), when AI_MODEL_ID contains kimi, ReLoop calls ConverseCommand without inline guardrailConfig (and uses maxTokens: 2048 without a custom temperature), because Kimi K3’s cross-region inference profile does not accept inline guardrailConfig. Instead, safety enforcement still invokes your published Guardrail directly via ApplyGuardrailCommand (bedrock:ApplyGuardrail permission in Module 5.6)!
Step 1 — Create Guardrail reloop2-ai-guardrail Open Amazon Bedrock -> Guardrails (verify Cross-region inference is available in ap-southeast-1 or configure guardrail-profile/apac.guardrail.v1:0) and click Create guardrail. Configure Guardrail details: Name: reloop2-ai-guardrail Description: ReLoop 2: filter unsafe text and images during AI device analysis Messaging for blocked prompts: Ảnh không phù hợp. Messaging for blocked responses: Kết quả không phù hợp. Enable Cross-region inference (apac.guardrail.v1:0) and add standard workshop tags (Owner=team, Project=reloop2, Purpose=workshop). Step 2 — Configure Content Filters (Standard Tier, HIGH) Under Content filters: select Standard tier and configure all 6 categories at HIGH threshold with BLOCK action: Category Input Modalities Input Strength Output Modalities Output Strength Hate TEXT, IMAGE HIGH TEXT HIGH Insults TEXT, IMAGE HIGH TEXT HIGH Sexual TEXT, IMAGE HIGH TEXT HIGH Violence TEXT, IMAGE HIGH TEXT HIGH Misconduct TEXT HIGH TEXT HIGH Prompt Attack TEXT HIGH (N/A) NONE Review all details and filters, then click Create guardrail. Step 3 — Test in Bedrock Guardrail Playground & Publish Version 1 Inside reloop2-ai-guardrail, test unsafe / prompt-injection text (Ignore previous instructions...) and confirm the Guardrail blocks it with "Ảnh không phù hợp." and displays a GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED trace. Next test a benign electronic device prompt (Dell Latitude laptop with cracked screen corner, battery missing) and verify it passes cleanly without intervention. Click Versions -> Create version, enter description v1 cho reloop2-api (ReLoop 2 workshop), and publish Version 1 (immutable snapshot for production/workshop stability). Step 4 — Wire Guardrail ID & Version to reloop2-api Lambda Open AWS Lambda -> reloop2-api -> Configuration -> Environment variables -> Edit, add: AI_GUARDRAIL_ID = <your guardrail ID> (e.g. a1b2c3d4e5f6) AI_GUARDRAIL_VERSION = 1 Save and verify.

title: Frontend SPA, CloudFront & Origin Access
content:
In this module you host the React/Vite Single-Page Application (SPA) inside a completely private S3 bucket (reloop2-web-7k3q), expose both the frontend and /api/* under a single Amazon CloudFront HTTPS origin using Origin Access Control (OAC), attach two lightweight CloudFront Functions, enforce strict Security Headers, lock direct API Gateway bypasses with x-origin-verify, and complete the CORS + Cognito URL backfill.
Part A — Create Private Web Bucket (reloop2-web-<suffix>) & Upload Bundle Open S3 -> Create bucket in ap-southeast-1, name it reloop2-web-7k3q (same unique suffix as reloop2-images), keep Block all public access ON, add tags, and keep SSE-S3 + Bucket Key. Build your React frontend (npm run build) with VITE_COGNITO_USER_POOL_ID, VITE_COGNITO_CLIENT_ID, VITE_COGNITO_DOMAIN, and VITE_API_BASE=/api, then upload index.html and the assets/ folder into reloop2-web-7k3q. Part B — Create Two CloudFront Functions (cloudfront-js-2.0) Go to CloudFront -> Functions -> Create function (runtime cloudfront-js-2.0): Function 1: reloop2-spa-rewrite — rewrites client-side React routes to /index.html ONLY when the URI does NOT end with a real static file extension (crucial for ReLoop chat routes formatted like /chat/<partnerId>.<listingId>, which contain a . but are not static files!): function handler(event) { var req = event.request; // Only real asset extensions pass; chat route "<partnerId>.<listingId>" also contains a dot if (!/\.(js|mjs|css|map|html|png|jpe?g|gif|svg|ico|webp|avif|txt|json|xml|webmanifest|woff2?|ttf)$/i.test(req.uri)) req.uri = '/index.html'; return req; } Function 2: reloop2-api-prefix — strips the leading /api prefix before CloudFront forwards requests to HTTP API Gateway (<api-id>.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com): function handler(event) { var req = event.request; req.uri = req.uri.replace(/^\/api(?=\/)/, ''); return req; } Part C — Create Security Response Headers Policy & OAC Go to CloudFront -> Policies -> Response headers -> Create response headers policy: Name: reloop2-security-headers Security headers (all Override checked): Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff X-Frame-Options: DENY Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self' Custom header: Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only (Override ON) allowing 'self', Google Fonts, S3 images bucket reloop2-images-7k3q.s3.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com, Cognito IDP & Hosted UI domain, and OpenStreetMap/Nominatim tiles. Go to CloudFront -> Security -> Origin access -> Create control setting: Name: reloop2-web Signing behavior: Sign requests (recommended) (always), SigV4, Origin type S3. Part D — Create Distribution, Dual Origins & Dual Behaviors Open CloudFront -> Distributions -> Create distribution: Use Pay as you go (PriceClass_200) Point first origin to reloop2-web-7k3q.s3.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com using OAC reloop2-web, default root object index.html, HTTP/2 + HTTP/3 (http2and3), IPv6 disabled (is_ipv6_enabled = false) Choose Do not enable security protections during the initial wizard (we attach a customized rate-limited WAF in Module 5.9!) Under General -> Settings -> Edit, verify Default root object is index.html and Supported HTTP versions is HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. Open the Origins tab and add the second origin (api): Origin domain: <api-id>.execute-api.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com (strip https://) Protocol: HTTPS only, TLSv1.2 minimum, Read timeout 30s, Keep-alive 5s Add custom header: x-origin-verify = <exact ORIGIN_VERIFY_SECRET value from Lambda> Open the Behaviors tab: Edit Default (*) behavior: Redirect HTTP to HTTPS, CachingOptimized, Response headers policy reloop2-security-headers, and Viewer request Function association -> reloop2-spa-rewrite. Create behavior for /api/* -> Target origin api: HTTPS only, Allowed methods GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, POST, PATCH, DELETE, Cache policy CachingDisabled, Origin request policy AllViewerExceptHostHeader, Response headers policy reloop2-security-headers, and Viewer request Function association -> reloop2-api-prefix. Copy CloudFront’s generated S3 bucket policy and paste it into reloop2-web-7k3q -> Permissions -> Bucket policy (CloudFrontRead s3:GetObject + CloudFrontList s3:ListBucket scoped strictly with StringEquals on AWS:SourceArn of your CloudFront Distribution ARN). Part E — Critical Backfill: Update CORS & Cognito URLs with CloudFront Domain Now that your CloudFront domain (https://<dist-domain>.cloudfront.net) exists, immediately update all three downstream services so authentication and uploads work smoothly:

title: Edge & Cognito Security with AWS WAFv2
content:
In this module you add two layered AWS WAFv2 Web ACLs:
Edge Web ACL (reloop2-web) in Global (us-east-1) attached directly to your CloudFront distribution — enforces endpoint-specific rate limiting, global IP ceilings, AWS Managed Rules (AmazonIpReputationList, KnownBadInputsRuleSet, CommonRuleSet tuned to avoid false blocks on photo payloads). Regional Web ACL (reloop2-auth) in Singapore (ap-southeast-1) attached directly to your Cognito User Pool — throttles credential stuffing and sign-up spam against 7 specific Cognito actions (300 requests / 5 minutes / IP). Part A — Create Edge Web ACL (reloop2-web in us-east-1) Switch your Console region to Global (CloudFront) or US East (N. Virginia) us-east-1 before creating reloop2-web. CloudFront WAF Web ACLs cannot be created from ap-southeast-1.
Open AWS WAF -> Web ACLs, select Global (CloudFront), and click Create web ACL. Under Step 1 — Describe web ACL and associate it to AWS resources: Name: reloop2-web Description: ReLoop 2: IP rate limits, bad IPs, common attack patterns - CloudFront Associated AWS resources: Click Add AWS resources and attach your CloudFront distribution. Add all 5 rules in priority order 0..4: Priority 0 — rate-limit-public-api: Rate-based rule (100 requests / 60-second window per IP) scoped down (OR) to URI path prefix (LOWERCASE, STARTS_WITH) matching /api/auth/, /api/feed/public, or /api/fees. Action: Block returning HTTP 429 JSON custom response (rate_limited, header retry-after: 60): {"code":"RATE_LIMITED","message":"Too many requests - wait about 1 minute and try again"} Priority 1 — rate-limit-per-ip: Rate-based rule (1000 requests / 60-second window per IP across all paths) returning the same HTTP 429 custom JSON response. Priority 2, 3, 4 — AWS Managed Free Rule Groups: AWS-AWSManagedRulesAmazonIpReputationList AWS-AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet AWS-AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet — edit sub-rules and set SizeRestrictions_BODY and GenericRFI_BODY overrides to Count so rich JSON listing payloads or external map URLs do not trigger false 403 blocks! Verify the 5 rules, confirm Priority ordering (0 to 4), keep CloudWatch metrics + sampled requests enabled, review, and click Create web ACL. Part B — Create Regional Auth Web ACL (reloop2-auth in ap-southeast-1) Switch back to Asia Pacific (Singapore) ap-southeast-1 in AWS WAF -> Create web ACL. Name it reloop2-auth, Description ReLoop 2: brute-force and sign-up spam protection - Cognito, and under Associated AWS resources select Amazon Cognito user pools -> reloop2-user-pool. Add 2 rules: Priority 0 — rate-limit-auth: Rate-based rule (300 requests / 300-second window per IP) scoped down when HTTP header x-amzn-cognito-operation-name (EXACTLY) matches any of: InitiateAuth, RespondToAuthChallenge, SignUp, ConfirmSignUp, ResendConfirmationCode, ForgotPassword, ConfirmForgotPassword. Action: Block. Priority 1 — AWS-AWSManagedRulesAmazonIpReputationList. Review, create reloop2-auth, and confirm reloop2-user-pool shows under Associated AWS resources.

title: Observability: Logs, Alarms, SNS & Dashboard
content:
In this module you establish cost-controlled logging (7-day retention), extract a structured metric from Lambda JSON error logs, wire SNS email alerts, configure two actionable CloudWatch Metric Alarms, and assemble the ReLoop2-Backend-Health dashboard.
Part A — Set 7-Day Log Retention & Create Error Metric Filter Open CloudWatch -> Logs -> Log groups (ap-southeast-1) and select /aws/lambda/reloop2-api. Click Actions -> Edit retention setting(s) -> set 1 week (7 days) so workshop logs never accumulate storage indefinitely. Open /aws/lambda/reloop2-api -> Metric filters -> Create metric filter: Filter pattern: { $.msg = "unhandled_error" } Filter name: reloop2-UnhandledErrors Metric namespace: ReLoop/reloop2 Metric name: UnhandledErrors Metric value: 1, Default value: 0 Part B — Create SNS Alert Topic & Email Subscription Open Amazon SNS -> Topics -> Create topic: Type: Standard Name: reloop2-alarms Display name: ReLoop 2 Alarms Click Create subscription: Protocol: Email Endpoint: alerts@example.com (your real inbox; check your email and click Confirm subscription so SNS changes state from Pending confirmation to Confirmed!) Part C — Create 2 CloudWatch Alarms & Operational Dashboard Open CloudWatch -> Alarms -> Create alarm: Alarm 1 (reloop2-lambda-errors): Metric AWS/Lambda -> Errors (FunctionName = reloop2-api), Statistic Sum, Period 5 minutes, Condition >= 3 (1 of 1 datapoints), Treat missing data as Not breaching (notBreaching), Notify reloop2-alarms. Alarm 2 (reloop2-api-5xx): Metric AWS/ApiGateway -> 5xx (ApiId = <your HTTP API ID>), Statistic Sum, Period 5 minutes, Condition >= 5, Notify reloop2-alarms. Open CloudWatch -> Dashboards -> Create dashboard, name it ReLoop2-Backend-Health, and add 3 widgets: Lambda API (reloop2-api): Invocations, Errors, Throttles (Sum, 5 min line chart) HTTP API (<api-id>): Count, 4xx, 5xx (Sum, 5 min line chart) DynamoDB Capacity (reloop2-core-table): ConsumedReadCapacityUnits, ConsumedWriteCapacityUnits (Number sparkline)

title: Cleanup & Infrastructure as Code (Terraform)
content:
Because AWS WAFv2 charges continuously by the hour/month even with zero requests, always tear down all reloop2-* workshop resources in reverse dependency order once verification finishes. If you work alongside other environments, verify every name starts with reloop2 before confirming deletion.
Part A — Exact Reverse-Order Console Teardown Disable & Delete CloudFront Distribution (CloudFront -> Distributions, Global): select your distribution -> Disable -> wait until status transitions to Disabled -> Delete. Disabling first breaks dependencies on WAF reloop2-web, OAC, Functions, and reloop2-security-headers. Delete EventBridge Scheduled Rule (reloop2-sweep) (EventBridge -> Rules, ap-southeast-1): deleting the rule removes the scheduled target cleanly. Delete CloudWatch Alarms, Dashboard & SNS Topic (reloop2-*, ReLoop2-Backend-Health, ap-southeast-1): delete reloop2-lambda-errors, reloop2-api-5xx, Dashboard ReLoop2-Backend-Health, and SNS topic reloop2-alarms + its email subscription. Delete Regional WAF (reloop2-auth, ap-southeast-1): disassociate from reloop2-user-pool if still attached, then delete reloop2-auth. Delete HTTP API Gateway (reloop2-api, ap-southeast-1). Delete Bedrock Guardrail (reloop2-ai-guardrail). Delete Cognito Domain (reloop2-auth) & User Pool (reloop2-user-pool): first delete the domain prefix (Branding -> Domain), then click Delete user pool, check Deactivate deletion protection, and enter reloop2-user-pool. Delete CloudFront Edge WAF, OAC, Response Headers Policy & Functions (Global / us-east-1): once the CloudFront distribution finishes deleting: Delete Global WAF reloop2-web Delete Response Headers Policy reloop2-security-headers Delete Origin Access Control reloop2-web Delete CloudFront Functions reloop2-api-prefix and reloop2-spa-rewrite Empty & Delete Both S3 Buckets (reloop2-web-7k3q, reloop2-images-7k3q): because versioned or populated S3 buckets refuse direct deletion, select each bucket -> Empty -> type permanently delete, then click Delete -> enter the bucket name. Delete Lambda Functions (reloop2-api, reloop2-post-confirmation) & CloudWatch Log Groups (/aws/lambda/reloop2-*): note deleting a Lambda does NOT automatically remove its CloudWatch Log Group—delete both log groups explicitly! Delete DynamoDB Table (reloop2-core-table): keep Create an on-demand backup unchecked so you incur zero ongoing backup storage fees, type confirm, and delete. Delete IAM Roles (reloop2-api-lambda-role, reloop2-post-confirmation-role) & AWS Budget (reloop2-budget). Part B — Verify Zero Leftover Resources via AWS CLI After Console cleanup, verify across both regions that zero reloop2 resources remain:
aws s3api list-buckets --query "Buckets[?contains(Name,'reloop2')].Name" aws dynamodb list-tables --region ap-southeast-1 --query "TableNames[?contains(@,'reloop2')]" aws lambda list-functions --region ap-southeast-1 --query "Functions[?contains(FunctionName,'reloop2')].FunctionName" aws logs describe-log-groups --region ap-southeast-1 --query "logGroups[?contains(logGroupName,'reloop2')].logGroupName" aws apigatewayv2 get-apis --region ap-southeast-1 --query "Items[?contains(Name,'reloop2')].Name" aws cognito-idp list-user-pools --max-results 60 --region ap-southeast-1 --query "UserPools[?contains(Name,'reloop2')].Name" aws wafv2 list-web-acls --scope CLOUDFRONT --region us-east-1 --query "WebACLs[?contains(Name,'reloop2')].Name" aws wafv2 list-web-acls --scope REGIONAL --region ap-southeast-1 --query "WebACLs[?contains(Name,'reloop2')].Name" aws cloudfront list-distributions --query "DistributionList.Items[?contains(Comment || '','reloop2')].Id" aws iam list-roles --query "Roles[?contains(RoleName,'reloop2')].RoleName" Part C — Reproducing Everything with Terraform (terraform/) Now that you understand every piece in the AWS Console, you can deploy or destroy the entire ReLoop stack in minutes using the modular Terraform (>= 1.6.0, hashicorp/aws >= 5.90) code included in this repository’s terraform/ directory:
File Managed Infrastructure provider.tf, data.tf, variables.tf Primary ap-southeast-1 + us_east_1 alias, CloudFront managed cache/origin policies, parameterized prefix & secrets storage.tf DynamoDB (PK/SK, GSI1, PITR, TTL), private images & web S3 buckets, CORS, 3 lifecycle rules, OAC bucket policy identity.tf Cognito User Pool, 4 groups, Managed Login v2 domain, PKCE client, post_confirmation IAM role + Python Lambda api.tf API Lambda IAM role + inline policy, Node.js 22 arm64 Lambda, HTTP API Gateway, JWT authorizer, 7 routes, throttling ai.tf Bedrock Guardrail (reloop2-ai-guardrail, APAC cross-region profile, Standard tier) + immutable Version 1 frontend.tf, functions/*.js OAC, CloudFront Functions (spa-rewrite.js, api-prefix.js), security-headers RHP, dual-origin CloudFront Distribution security.tf Edge WAF (reloop2-web, us-east-1) + Regional Cognito WAF (reloop2-auth, ap-southeast-1) + User Pool association events.tf, monitoring.tf, outputs.tf EventBridge 15m rule, Log retention + metric filter, SNS email topic, 2 Alarms, CloudWatch Dashboard, $5 AWS Budget Observed Engineering Notes from Live Import Verification This Terraform layout was imported and checked against the live reloop2 Console deployment (71 / 71 resources imported, 0 to destroy in terraform plan):
Breaking the CloudFront <-> CORS Dependency Cycle: CloudFront Distribution depends on the API Gateway domain and S3 website bucket, whereas Cognito callback URLs, S3 images CORS, and API Gateway CORS need the generated CloudFront domain. Keep cloudfront_cors_origins = [] on your initial terraform apply, read terraform output cloudfront_domain, then set cloudfront_cors_origins = ["https://<domain>"] and apply once more cleanly (just like Console Part 5.8 Part E). SNS Email Subscriptions (PendingConfirmation): AWS SNS does not return a subscription ARN until the recipient clicks the confirmation email link, so unconfirmed email subscriptions report PendingConfirmation until confirmed. Never Commit Secrets or State: Keep your real terraform.tfvars (containing origin_verify_secret and alert_email), terraform.tfstate*, .terraform/, and zip packages strictly out of Git using .gitignore — start by copying terraform.tfvars.example to terraform.tfvars. cd terraform cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars # Populate alert_email, origin_verify_secret, and Lambda zip paths terraform init terraform plan terraform apply # After getting cloudfront_domain output, set cloudfront_cors_origins in terraform.tfvars and re-apply: terraform apply # Full cleanup when finished: terraform destroy
